chapter_title: Concerning the Fifty Lord's Days; to what Mysteries do they correspond? Or the Second (Fifty); to whose Sign (are they)?
chapter_note: This chapter is primarily institutional — its purpose is to explain church fasting practices (fifty lord's days for catechumens, fifty for elect) by grounding them in cosmic mysteries. The oldest teaching substrate is concentrated in paragraphs 2-4, which describe the First Man's five garments with five powers each, the summons and obedience, and the cosmic food cycle. This substrate cosmological material (the five-fold multiplication yielding 25, doubled to 50 by the call-and-answer pair) has been appropriated to justify institutional fasting schedules. The second half of the chapter (P5-8) shows strong editorial fatigue — institutional vocabulary dominates as the chapter pivots to Gospel narrative (Christ's forty days fasting, seven at Simon's house, three in the tomb) and Mani's first-person institutional claims. The substrate fragments preserved here are genuine (five-garments teaching, summons/obedience emanation pair, cosmic living food) but are embedded in a thoroughly institutional framework.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Combines dialogue frame formula ('Once again a disciple stood up... I beseech you, my master') with entirely institutional question content: 'fifty lord's days,' 'catechumens fast,' 'the elect.' The question defines the chapter's institutional purpose. No cosmological content in the question itself — it asks about church practice, not cosmic structure.

paragraphs.core_text: [In eac]h one of these five garments that the [First] Man summoned there are five powers. They shall be counted to the [ ... each] other, these five, and five times [ ... ] their number. However, at the time [ ... ] the summons went down. The answer wished to ascend with it. And the summons with the obedience [constitute] twenty-five characteristics in their twenty-five limbs, [which] are the sons of the Man. The summons and [the obed]ience were raised to the heights through them.
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed dialogue frame 'Then [he] says to his questioner and they with him:' (editorial attribution) and dialogic address 'Happen you know that' (second-person audience address, part of frame layer).
paragraphs.temporal_note: Core substrate teaching: the five-garments-of-the-First-Man with five powers each (5×5 structure) is a fundamental cosmological-correspondential pattern found across the Kephalaia. The summons and obedience (call and answer) as a cosmic emanation pair yielding the 25 characteristics mapped to 25 limbs — this is systematic cosmic architecture where both sides stay within the system. The mathematical structure (5×5=25) is characteristic of the oldest layer's degree-mapping method.

paragraphs.core_text: ⟨p.263⟩ Just as their fa[ther] the living Man raised himself up through them, by these these other ones have set up all things a[bov]e and below. They fasted from their [foo]d, [w]hich is their own.
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed 'Indeed, these are what are called pentecost, the fifty great days that are the [archetypes of the] holy [d]ays.' — editorial bridge connecting cosmic numerology to the institutional pentecost observance. One side of the mapping (cosmic fifty) reaches into the compilers' religious calendar ('pentecost,' 'holy days').
paragraphs.temporal_note: The substrate elements describe cosmic process: the living Man's ascent, the setting up of all things above and below, cosmic beings fasting from their own food (abstaining from the food of life in the world of mixture). Both sides of these mappings stay within the cosmic system. The editorial bridge sentence interrupts the cosmic narrative with institutional identification.

paragraphs.core_text: So, from that time until [the time] of [the adv]ent of Jesus the Splendour, the glorious one who came [ ... / ... t]heir food which is the [ ... ] of sou[l], which is the summons and the obedience [ ... ] that spiritual food. They rele[ased ... ] all these fifty days, which [ ... ] this living food suffices for all of them. It filled them all with power and richness and life. Light [ ... ] this living food that [ ... ] became rich.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Describes the cosmic food cycle: spiritual food identified as the summons and obedience, living food that fills with power/richness/life. Both sides of the mappings stay within the cosmic system (cosmic food → cosmic nourishment). 'Jesus the Splendour' is a cosmological entity in the Manichaean system (the cosmic awakener of the Third Evocation); the NAME may be a Manichaean overlay on an older substrate cosmic figure, but the teaching about living food and spiritual nourishment is substrate vocabulary. Heavy lacunae make certainty difficult. The temporal framing ('from that time until the advent of...') integrates this into cosmic narrative rather than institutional practice.

Transitional paragraph connecting cosmic fifty to institutional hundred days. 'The one hundred holy days,' 'the elect fast,' 'these mysteries of these first fifty' — the paragraph's function is institutional: explaining why there are two sets of fifty fasting days. Substrate vocabulary appears ('the summons and the obedience set them in their splendrous places at the coming of Jesus') but is embedded in and subordinate to the institutional framework. Heavily damaged, making clean extraction impossible. The paragraph bridges from cosmic teaching (P2-4) to the institutional explanation (P6-8), marking the editorial fatigue boundary.

Flagged as probable editorial extension by seam detection. First-person institutional voice: 'I have revealed for the catechumens,' 'I have revealed for the elect.' References to 'the sects' and their pentecost practice. Claims apostolic precedent ('the apostles themselves fasted for these fifty days'). Entirely institutional — Mani establishing his fasting calendar by appeal to apostolic authority and polemical comparison with rival sects. No substrate content.

Gospel narrative applied to institutional fasting: Christ's forty days fasting on the mountain, seven days at Simon the leper's house, three days in the tomb = fifty days. This is a NT citation/calculation entering the text via Manichaean editorial construction. The 'second fifty' framework mapping onto Christ's biography is a Manichaean Christological construction, not substrate cosmological teaching.

First-person institutional claim: 'I, I have bestowed them on the entire church.' Summarizes the chapter's institutional scheme: catechumens' fifty after the First Man, elect's fifty after 'the second man who was revealed in the church.' 'The entire church,' 'catechumens fast,' 'revealed in the church' — saturated institutional vocabulary. The pairing of 'First Man' (cosmic) with 'second man' (Jesus/church) confirms editorial construction connecting substrate cosmology to institutional practice.
